COSTA-HAWKINS RENTAL HOUSING ACT — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for 123 Main St., San Diego, CA 92101 · Jordan Lee

INTRODUCTION AND SCOPE
This information sheet describes the Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act (Civil Code section 1954.50 et seq.), a 1995 California statute that limits the authority of local governments (cities and counties) to apply residential rent control to certain categories of housing, and that separately addresses the rent a landlord may charge a new tenant after a prior tenancy ends. It concerns the property commonly known as 123 Main St., San Diego, CA 92101, the tenancy of Jordan Lee, and the landlord Morgan Casey. If a current monthly rent figure is relevant, it is stated here as: $2,200.

Costa-Hawkins is a different, older statute from California's statewide Tenant Protection Act of 2019 (AB 1482, Civil Code sections 1946.2 and 1947.12), which is addressed in a separate information sheet in this collection. AB 1482 is itself a statewide substantive floor -- a rent-increase cap and a just-cause-for-termination requirement -- that applies directly to a tenancy. Costa-Hawkins works differently: rather than regulating a tenancy directly, it constrains what a city or county's own local rent-control ordinance is allowed to regulate, and it is the source of what is commonly called "vacancy decontrol." This document does not restate AB 1482's rent-cap or just-cause content, and it does not itself determine whether this or any other specific tenancy, unit, or local ordinance is covered by, or exempt from, Costa-Hawkins, AB 1482, or any local rent-control ordinance.

WHAT COSTA-HAWKINS DOES: A PREEMPTION STATUTE, NOT A RENT-CONTROL LAW
The Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act does not itself impose rent control; it constrains the residential rent control that a "public entity" -- a term with the same meaning given to it in Government Code section 811.2, which includes a city, a county, and other local governmental bodies -- may otherwise establish, continue, or enforce. Its central operative provisions are framed as overriding contrary local law: an owner "may establish the initial and all subsequent rental rates" for certain categories of housing, and separately "may establish the initial rental rate" when a tenancy turns over, in each case "notwithstanding any other provision of law" -- language that displaces a conflicting local rent-control ordinance rather than creating a new substantive rent-control scheme of its own. The statute's own terms confirm that its target is local law: one of its new-construction categories turns on whether a unit "has already been exempt from the residential rent control ordinance of a public entity" before a specified date.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "This chapter shall be known and may be cited as the Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1954.50 (California Legislative Information text), Civ. C. § 1954.50 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1954.50.)
  "“Public entity” has the same meaning as set forth in Section 811.2 of the Government Code."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1954.51(d) (California Legislative Information text), Civ. C. § 1954.51(d) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1954.51.)
  "(a) Notwithstanding any other provision of law, an owner of residential real property may establish the initial and all subsequent rental rates for a dwelling or a unit about which any of the following is true:"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1954.52(a) (California Legislative Information text), Civ. C. § 1954.52(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1954.52.)
  "(2) It has already been exempt from the residential rent control ordinance of a public entity on or before February 1, 1995, pursuant to a local exemption for newly constructed units."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1954.52(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text), Civ. C. § 1954.52(a)(2) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1954.52.)
  Known gap: This clause establishes only the statute's own framing of what it does -- constrain local ("public entity") rent control -- not a comprehensive description of every California city or county's rent-control ordinance, which vary widely and are not catalogued here. The citations to Civil Code section 1954.52(a) (the preemption clause) and section 1954.52(a)(2) (the public-entity cross-reference) are both to the same statutory section and are treated here as one source, not as independently corroborating sources; the citations to section 1954.50 (short title) and section 1954.51(d) (definition of "public entity") are to separate, independently numbered sections. This document addresses Costa-Hawkins only; it is a different, older statute from the statewide Tenant Protection Act of 2019 (AB 1482), which is addressed in a separate information sheet and is not restated here. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's rent-control-preemption framework -- not a claim about which state's law governs any specific tenancy; landlord-tenant rules vary significantly by state. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine whether any specific local ordinance, unit, or tenancy is covered by, or exempt from, this chapter.

THE SINGLE-FAMILY HOME / CONDOMINIUM ("ALIENABLE TITLE") EXEMPTION
Civil Code section 1954.52(a)(3) exempts from local rent control a dwelling or unit that "is alienable separate from the title to any other dwelling unit" -- a category that commonly includes single-family homes and condominium units that can be sold on their own, separate from a larger building -- or that is a subdivided interest in a subdivision as specified in the cross-referenced Business and Professions Code provision. That exemption does not apply, however, in either of two situations: where the preceding tenancy was terminated by the owner using a notice under Civil Code section 1946.1, or was ended by an owner-noticed change in the terms of the tenancy under Civil Code section 827; or, for a condominium specifically, where the unit has not yet been sold separately by the subdivider to a bona fide purchaser for value.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "(3) (A) It is alienable separate from the title to any other dwelling unit or is a subdivided interest in a subdivision, as specified in subdivision (b), (d), or (f) of Section 11004.5 of the Business and Professions Code."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1954.52(a)(3)(A) (California Legislative Information text), Civ. C. § 1954.52(a)(3)(A) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1954.52.)
  "(B) This paragraph does not apply to either of the following: (i) A dwelling or unit where the preceding tenancy has been terminated by the owner by notice pursuant to Section 1946.1 or has been terminated upon a change in the terms of the tenancy noticed pursuant to Section 827. (ii) A condominium dwelling or unit that has not been sold separately by the subdivider to a bona fide purchaser for value."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1954.52(a)(3)(B) (California Legislative Information text), Civ. C. § 1954.52(a)(3)(B) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1954.52.)
  Known gap: This exemption is a Costa-Hawkins-specific provision, distinct from the differently worded and differently conditioned alienable-title exemption found in the statewide Tenant Protection Act of 2019 (Civil Code sections 1947.12(d)(5) and 1946.2(e)(8)), which is addressed in a separate information sheet in this collection; this clause does not restate that statute's ownership-type conditions (excluding REITs, corporations, and certain LLCs) or its required tenant-notice language, because Civil Code section 1954.52(a)(3) does not itself contain either of those conditions. The two citations below (subparagraphs (A) and (B)) are both from subdivision (a)(3) of the same statutory section (Civil Code section 1954.52) and are treated here as one source, not as independently corroborating sources. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's rent-control-preemption framework -- not a claim about which state's law governs any specific tenancy; landlord-tenant rules vary significantly by state. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine whether any specific dwelling or unit qualifies for, or has lost, this exemption.

THE NEW-CONSTRUCTION EXEMPTION
Civil Code section 1954.52(a) exempts new construction from local rent control in two alternative ways, not one single statewide cutoff date. The first is a fixed statewide date: a dwelling or unit with a certificate of occupancy issued after February 1, 1995 qualifies. The second is tied instead to a specific local ordinance's own terms: a dwelling or unit that had already been exempted from a public entity's residential rent control ordinance on or before February 1, 1995, under that ordinance's own preexisting local exemption for newly constructed units, also qualifies -- regardless of when the unit's certificate of occupancy actually issued. Because this second pathway depends on whether, and as of when, a given city or county's own ordinance already exempted new construction, the practical effect of the new-construction exemption is not identical from one local rent-control jurisdiction to the next.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "(1) It has a certificate of occupancy issued after February 1, 1995."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1954.52(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), Civ. C. § 1954.52(a)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1954.52.)
  "(2) It has already been exempt from the residential rent control ordinance of a public entity on or before February 1, 1995, pursuant to a local exemption for newly constructed units."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1954.52(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text), Civ. C. § 1954.52(a)(2) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1954.52.)
  Known gap: This clause states the statutory mechanism only; it does not determine the certificate-of-occupancy issuance date for any specific unit, and it does not catalog which California cities' or counties' rent-control ordinances had a newly-constructed-units exemption in effect on or before February 1, 1995, or what that local exemption's own terms were -- both are fact-specific inquiries this document does not undertake. The two citations below (paragraphs (1) and (2)) are both from subdivision (a) of the same statutory section (Civil Code section 1954.52) and are treated here as one source, not as independently corroborating sources. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's rent-control-preemption framework -- not a claim about which state's law governs any specific tenancy; landlord-tenant rules vary significantly by state. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine whether any specific dwelling or unit qualifies for this exemption.

VACANCY DECONTROL: RESETTING RENT BETWEEN TENANCIES
Civil Code section 1954.53(a) allows an owner to establish the initial rental rate for a dwelling or unit when a tenancy ends -- "notwithstanding any other provision of law," meaning notwithstanding a contrary local rent-control ordinance -- except where the owner itself ended the preceding tenancy by a notice under Civil Code section 1946.1 or changed its terms by a notice under Civil Code section 827. Because that exception covers an owner-initiated no-fault termination, the practical effect is that an owner may reset the rent to a new figure of the owner's choosing where the prior tenant vacated voluntarily or was evicted for cause, but not where the owner itself forced the vacancy through a no-fault termination notice. Once set, that new rate applies for the entire tenancy that follows, including any renewal by the same tenant. The statute also addresses a partial change in occupancy: if the original occupants no longer permanently reside in the unit, the owner may raise the rent for a new sublessee or assignee who did not live there before January 1, 1996 -- but this increase does not apply where one or more of the original occupants remains in lawful possession of the unit, or where a sublessee or assignee who already resided there before January 1, 1996 remains in possession.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "(a) Notwithstanding any other provision of law, an owner of residential real property may establish the initial rental rate for a dwelling or unit, except where any of the following applies: (1) The previous tenancy has been terminated by the owner by notice pursuant to Section 1946.1 or has been terminated upon a change in the terms of the tenancy noticed pursuant to Section 827, except a change permitted by law in the amount of rent or fees."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1954.53(a) (California Legislative Information text), Civ. C. § 1954.53(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1954.53.)
  "(b) Subdivision (a) applies to, and includes, renewal of the initial hiring by the same tenant, lessee, authorized subtenant, or authorized sublessee for the entire period of their occupancy at the rental rate established for the initial hiring."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1954.53(b) (California Legislative Information text), Civ. C. § 1954.53(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1954.53.)
  "(2) If the original occupant or occupants who took possession of the dwelling or unit pursuant to the rental agreement with the owner no longer permanently reside there, an owner may increase the rent by any amount allowed by this section to a lawful sublessee or assignee who did not reside at the dwelling or unit prior to January 1, 1996."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1954.53(d)(2) (California Legislative Information text), Civ. C. § 1954.53(d)(2) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1954.53.)
  "(3) This subdivision does not apply to partial changes in occupancy of a dwelling or unit where one or more of the occupants of the premises, pursuant to the agreement with the owner provided for above, remains an occupant in lawful possession of the dwelling or unit, or where a lawful sublessee or assignee who resided at the dwelling or unit prior to January 1, 1996, remains in possession of the dwelling or unit."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1954.53(d)(3) (California Legislative Information text), Civ. C. § 1954.53(d)(3) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1954.53.)
  Known gap: This clause does not reproduce every condition in Civil Code section 1954.53 -- for example, its separate provisions addressing units affected by prior governmental rent-limitation contracts, physically-disabled tenants' right to move within a property, security-deposit handling, or units cited for uncorrected serious health, safety, fire, or building code violations. The four citations below (subdivisions (a), (b), and (d)(2)-(3)) are all from the same statutory section (Civil Code section 1954.53) and are treated here as one source, not as independently corroborating sources. This document uses the commonly used term "vacancy decontrol" as a description of this mechanism; that phrase does not itself appear in the statutory text quoted here. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's rent-control-preemption framework -- not a claim about which state's law governs any specific tenancy; landlord-tenant rules vary significantly by state. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine whether this or any other specific rent reset, or any specific unit or tenancy, complies with, or is covered by, this section.
